The town clock had been wrong for as long as anyone could remember, and the people had made peace with it. Shops opened when the baker's bell rang, school began when the first crow landed on the fence, and meetings started whenever everyone had finished their tea. Visitors found it maddening, but they usually left a little slower and a little lighter, and some of them came back.

They complain for a week, then rebuild the fences, plant new rows beside the water, and pretend it was all part of the plan from the start. The river, naturally, says nothing at all.

Children whispered at the shelves, a student fell asleep over a thick atlas, and an elderly man read the same page of poetry three times, smiling a little more each time, as if the words were an old friend arriving late.

She measured flour with a chipped teacup, judged the oven by holding her hand near the door, and said the dough would tell me when it was ready. I laughed then, but years later, alone in my own kitchen, the dough spoke up, and I understood exactly what she had meant, and I wrote nothing down either.

By the third week the maps were soaked, the compass was sulking, and the youngest member had learned to sleep standing up. They reached the pass in a blizzard, and nobody could say afterwards whether they had been brave or merely too tired to turn around.

Good software is mostly patient listening. You ask what the person is trying to do, watch where they hesitate, and fix the small thing that makes them sigh. The big features get the attention, but it is the quiet removal of ten tiny annoyances that makes a tool feel like it was built by someone who has actually used it, on a bad day, with a deadline.

At the edge of the city there is a hill where nothing was ever built, and on summer evenings half the neighbourhood climbs it with blankets and flasks. They watch the lights come on below, point out the roofs they know, and argue cheerfully about which window is which. Then the stars arrive, the arguing stops, and everyone simply looks up in the warm dark.

The ferry captain had a rule: no one gets off until they have said something kind to a stranger. It started as a joke, but passengers took it seriously, and soon the crossing was full of quiet compliments about hats, dogs, and sturdy umbrellas. On the far shore, people stepped onto the dock a little taller, and the captain pretended not to notice, polishing a brass rail that was already bright.

Winter arrived overnight, and the village woke to a world with all its edges rounded off. Roofs wore thick white caps, the pond had become a pale plate, and the church bell sounded softer, as if wrapped in wool. Children raced out in mismatched boots while their parents stood at the doors with warm mugs, deciding whether any work could possibly wait.

A friend once told me that waiting is only wasted if you refuse to look around. I tried it at the next bus stop and noticed the pattern in the brickwork, a sparrow arguing with a paper cup, and the kind way two strangers shared a bench. By the time the bus came, I almost wanted it to be a little later, which felt like a small and rather quiet victory that I told no one about.
